title: High-Rise and Apartment
intro: Living in a shared building changes almost every part of an emergency: water, elevators, stairs, fire, drains and door locks all depend on equipment you do not control. This module has you learn how your own building works, test your smoke alarms, read its fire safety plan, and put your questions to management before you need the answers.

actions.title: Ask management the questions on the Building information sheet
actions.why: Pumps, elevators, door locks and heating all depend on power you do not control, and only management can tell you what keeps running and for how long.
actions.how: Print the Building information sheet. Email or hand it to your building manager and ask for written answers. Follow up once after a week. File the answers with your plan. If the answers show that your floor depends on pumps, store your full water target at home and plan to fill containers the moment the power fails (X4-02). Carry the metal keys to your unit and the building, not only a fob. Visitors cannot buzz in during an outage, so agree to meet them at the door. Do not wait for the answers to save the after-hours or emergency maintenance number: it is usually posted in the lobby, by the elevators or in your lease. Save it in every household phone under Building emergency and write it on a note inside your front door. It is for building problems. For a fire or anyone in danger, call 911 first; for a gas smell, get everyone out before you call anyone (AR-13).
actions.done: Management's written answers on the Building information sheet are filed with your plan, or you have sent the sheet and followed up once.

actions.title: Press the test button on your smoke alarm
actions.why: A smoke alarm with a dead battery gives no warning, and one press tells you whether yours works.
actions.how: Press and hold the test button on the smoke alarm nearest your bed until it sounds, then let go. If it stays silent, change the battery, or tell your landlord today if it is wired in.
actions.done: The alarm sounded, or you have changed the battery or sent your landlord a message today.

actions.title: Check each place has a smoke alarm that sounds when tested
actions.why: Working smoke alarms cut the risk of dying in a home fire by more than half.
actions.how: Walk through your home and check there is a smoke alarm inside each bedroom, outside each sleeping area and on every level. Outside a sleeping area or on a level, a combination smoke and carbon monoxide alarm does both jobs (HC-22); a bedroom still needs its own smoke alarm. Press and hold each test button until it sounds, and do it monthly from now on. If one stays silent, change its battery. Read the date on the back and replace any alarm that is more than 10 years past its date of manufacture; replace 9-volt backup batteries once a year. Never take the battery out to silence an alarm. If you have drawn a sketch of your home (U2-98), mark each alarm on it and note any room that has none. In a rented home, report a missing or dead alarm to the landlord in writing today.
actions.done: A smoke alarm inside each bedroom, outside each sleeping area and on every level sounded when tested, and none is more than 10 years past its date.
actions.apartment: Alarms wired into the building are the landlord's: report a dead or missing one in writing, never disconnect it, and add your own battery alarm in any bedroom that has none. Alarms in hallways and stairwells belong to the building; if one is chirping or missing, tell management.

actions.title: Sleep with the bedroom door closed
actions.why: A closed door slows the spread of smoke, heat and fire, which can give you more time to wake and get out.
actions.how: Close every bedroom door at night, starting tonight. Then test the smoke alarm (HC-23) with the doors shut and check that every sleeper can hear it; if not, add an alarm inside the bedroom (HC-23). Agree who goes to children or to anyone who needs help if the alarm sounds.
actions.done: Bedroom doors are closed at night, every sleeper has heard the alarm test through a closed door, and it is agreed who goes to each child or person needing help.

actions.title: Read your building's fire safety plan
actions.why: Buildings differ on whether residents should leave or stay when the alarm sounds, and the plan is where your building's answer is written down.
actions.how: Look for the plan or fire safety notice on the back of your front door, in the lobby or by the elevators; if you cannot find one, ask management for a copy. Read it for five things: what the alarm means in your building (leave at once, or wait for an announcement), which stairs to use, where to meet outside, what to do if fire or smoke blocks your way, and what to do if you cannot use stairs. If anything is unclear, ask the manager, and ask about the alarms, sprinklers and voice announcements. If management has no plan to give you, HR-06 has a default to use until it does. Note the key points on the Building information sheet by hand.
actions.done: The key points of your building's fire safety plan are noted on the Building information sheet, or management has said it has no plan to give.

actions.title: Find out whether your building has sprinklers and what it is built of
actions.why: Sprinklers and fire-resistant construction decide how far a fire can spread, which is why fire plans differ from one building to the next.
actions.how: Ask management three things: are there sprinklers in every unit and hallway, or only in some areas; is the structure fire-resistive (concrete or protected steel) or combustible (wood frame); and is there a central alarm with voice announcements. Fire departments can give different instructions for fire-resistive and combustible buildings, so check which applies to you in your building's fire safety plan (HR-02). If the building has no sprinklers, ask the owners in writing to consider installing them. Write the answers on the Building information sheet by hand, and the building type on the Fire card for the inside of your front door. The answer sets your default in HR-06.
actions.done: Management's answers on sprinklers, structure and alarm are written on the Building information sheet, and the building type is written on the Fire card.

actions.title: Find the two stairwells nearest your door
actions.why: In a fire or an outage the stairs are your way out, and the nearest stairwell may be blocked by smoke.
actions.how: Step out of your front door now and follow the exit signs to the nearest stairwell door, then to the next nearest. Count the doors you pass between your own door and each stairwell, so you could find them in the dark. Never walk into smoke to follow the count. Tell everyone in your home both counts. If your floor has only one stairwell, note that and ask about it when you read the fire safety plan (HR-02).
actions.done: You have walked to both stairwell doors and can say how many doors you pass on the way to each.

actions.title: Walk each stairwell down to the street
actions.why: A stairwell you have walked once is one you can use in the dark, and the walk shows up locked or blocked doors while there is still time to fix them.
actions.how: Walk each of your stairwells from your floor to the outside, once. Count the flights, and note where the stairs come out (street, lobby, alley or garage) and whether the last door opens freely from inside. Check that stair doors are marked, close by themselves and are not locked, wedged open or blocked by stored things, and whether they lock behind you so that you cannot get back onto a floor. Report anything wrong to management in writing (HR-17), and note the exits on the Building information sheet by hand.
actions.done: You have walked each stairwell from your floor to the outside, and where each one comes out is noted on the Building information sheet.

actions.title: Learn what to do when the fire alarm sounds
actions.why: The right first move depends on where the fire is and what your building is made of, and there is no time to work that out once the alarm is ringing.
actions.how: Firefighters' instructions and any announcement come first, then your building's fire safety plan (HR-02). If you have neither, use the rule the New York City Fire Department teaches. Fire or smoke in your own home: get everyone out, close the door behind you, take the stairs, never the elevator, and call 911 from a safe place. Fire somewhere else in a fire-resistive building (concrete or protected steel): it is usually safer to stay in your home with the door closed, call 911 with your floor and unit, and follow the cannot-leave steps (HR-07); leave if smoke or heat comes into your home or you are told to. Fire somewhere else in a combustible building (wood frame): it is usually safer to leave at once. Whenever you leave, feel the door and the handle first. If the door is warm, do not open it. If it is cool, open it slowly; if the hallway is clear, close every door behind you and walk down the nearest stairs to your meeting place. Use your other stairwell only if the way to it is clear. Never walk into a smoke-filled hallway or stairwell to leave a fire that is somewhere else: go back in, close the door and follow HR-07.
actions.done: The Fire card on the inside of your front door shows which kind of building it is written for, and everyone at home has been shown it.

actions.title: Learn what to do if you cannot leave during a fire
actions.why: If fire or smoke blocks the way out, or you cannot manage the stairs, a closed door and a call to the fire department protect you until help arrives.
actions.how: Stay in your unit, or go back to it, and close every door between you and the smoke. Push wet towels or sheets into the gap around the door and over any vent where smoke comes in. Call 911 and give the building address, your floor and unit number, and how many people are with you; keep in contact, because clearing a tall building can take a long time. If smoke or flames are coming up the outside of the building from below you, keep the windows shut and signal through the glass with a flashlight. Otherwise open a window a few inches and wave a bright cloth or a flashlight so crews can see where you are, and close it again if smoke comes in. Never break a window, because you may need to close it.
actions.done: Every person at home has read the cannot-leave steps or heard them read aloud.

actions.title: Stay out of elevators in a fire or after an earthquake
actions.why: In a fire or after an earthquake an elevator can stop without warning and trap you where nobody can reach you quickly.
actions.how: Make it a household rule: whenever you leave during a fire (HR-06), or after any shaking, everyone takes the stairs, even if the elevator seems to be working. The only exceptions are when firefighters tell you to use an elevator, or your building has elevators clearly marked for emergency use and its fire safety plan says to use them. After any other emergency, stay off the elevators until management or officials say they are safe.
actions.done: Everyone at home has heard the household rule about elevators.

actions.title: Know what to do if you are stuck in an elevator
actions.why: People stuck in elevators are one of the first effects of a power outage, and the danger lies in trying to force a way out.
actions.how: Press the alarm or call button and use the intercom; if nobody answers, phone the building's after-hours number, and call 911 if anyone is ill or hurt. Then wait: sit down, save your phone battery, and never force the doors or climb out of the car. If you feel shaking while riding, press every floor button and get off at the first floor where the doors open. Save the after-hours number now (HR-01).
actions.done: The building's after-hours number is saved in every household phone, and everyone at home has heard the steps read aloud.

actions.title: Plan for anyone who cannot use the stairs
actions.why: When the elevators stop, a person who cannot manage stairs depends on a plan that other people already know about.
actions.how: Tell management in writing that someone in your unit cannot use stairs, and ask for that to be on the list the building gives to firefighters. Call the fire department's non-emergency line and ask whether it keeps a register of residents who need help. Ask two neighbors on your floor, by name, to check on the person and to tell fire crews where they are; write their names and numbers on the Floor contact list by hand. Agree where the person waits (in the unit with the door closed, or the place your fire safety plan names) and that they call 911 with the floor and unit number and say they cannot use the stairs.
actions.done: Management holds your written notice, two neighbors on your floor have said yes, and their names and numbers are written on the Floor contact list.

actions.title: Consider an evacuation chair if someone cannot manage stairs
actions.why: A stair chair lets one or two trained helpers bring a person down safely when the elevators are out and staying is not safe.
actions.how: Ask management first whether the building already keeps one, and where. If you buy your own, check its weight rating, whether it needs one helper or two, and that it fits the width of your stairs and landings. Practice with the helpers who would use it: first empty on one flight, then with the person strapped in. Store it by your door; in a fire, someone who cannot use the stairs calls 911 and waits behind a closed door unless in immediate danger (HR-07, X7-03).
actions.done: Management has told you where the building's chair is kept, or your own fits your stairs, is stored by your door and its helpers have practiced with it.

actions.title: Keep hallways, landings and stairs clear
actions.why: Anything stored on the escape route slows people down in the dark, and can burn.
actions.how: Keep nothing in the building hallway outside your door, on stair landings or in the stairwell: no shoe racks, bikes, strollers, boxes, plants or trash bags. Keep the hallway inside your unit clear from the bedrooms to the front door. Never wedge a stair or hallway fire door open, because closed doors keep smoke and fire out of the stairs. Ask management what may be kept in hose, riser and meter closets (usually nothing). If other people's things block the way, tell management.
actions.done: Nothing of yours is in the building hallway, on a stair landing or in the stairwell, and your own hallway is clear from the bedrooms to the front door.

actions.title: Close the door behind you when you leave a fire
actions.why: A closed door holds fire and smoke inside one unit and keeps the hallway and stairs usable for everyone else.
actions.how: If the fire is in your own home, get everyone out, take your keys, close the door of the burning room if you can do it safely, and pull your front door shut behind you. Pull the alarm station on your way to the stairs and call 911 from a safe place with the address, floor and unit. For a fire elsewhere in the building, HR-06 has the rule for staying or leaving and HR-07 the cannot-leave steps; in both you keep doors closed and never walk into smoke. Today, test your front door's closer: open the door fully and let go; it should swing shut and latch by itself, and if it does not, report it to management.
actions.done: Your front door swings shut and latches by itself when opened fully and let go, or management has your report that it does not.

actions.title: Know what your balcony is not for
actions.why: Grills, fuel and generators on a balcony put fire and carbon monoxide next to your own windows and your neighbors'.
actions.how: Never run a generator on a balcony: it must be outdoors and at least 20 feet from any window, door or vent, which no balcony allows. Do not grill on the balcony, and do not use or store charcoal, gas cylinders or liquid fuel there (see X3-05). Do not count on the balcony as a way out. Before strong wind, bring in or tie down furniture, plants and anything loose.
actions.done: No grill, charcoal, gas cylinder or liquid fuel is kept on your balcony.
actions.cite_todo: No registry source states a rule on grills or fuel on apartment balconies; the ban here is the site's city-safety rule.

actions.title: Learn the shut-offs inside your own unit
actions.why: A burst hose or a sparking appliance can be stopped in seconds if you know which valve or switch is yours.
actions.how: Find and label three things. 1) Your breaker panel: the main switch, and which breaker feeds which room. 2) Water shutoff valves: under every sink, behind the toilet, behind the washing machine and dishwasher, and a unit shut-off if you have one; they close clockwise. 3) The valve behind a gas stove or dryer, if you have one: ask management or the gas company how it closes. Turn each water valve off and on once so you know it moves, do not practice on the gas valve, and report any valve that is stuck or drips to management. Leaving comes before any valve: if you smell gas, follow the gas steps (AR-13). Everything beyond these (main lines, risers, meters, pumps, sprinklers) is not yours to touch (HR-25). Note the locations on the Building information sheet by hand.
actions.done: Your breakers, water shutoff valves and any gas appliance valve are labeled, each water valve has been turned off and on, and their locations are on the Building information sheet.

actions.title: Save the building's after-hours emergency number
actions.why: Floods, stuck elevators and failed door locks rarely happen in office hours, when the daytime number goes to voicemail.
actions.how: Find the after-hours or emergency maintenance number: it is usually posted in the lobby, by the elevators or in your lease, or ask management. Save it in every household phone under Building emergency, and write it by hand on the Building information sheet and on a note inside your front door. It is for building problems. For a fire or anyone in danger, call 911 first; for a gas smell, get everyone out before you call anyone (HR-15 has the rule).
actions.done: The after-hours number is saved in every household phone under Building emergency, and written on the Building information sheet and on a note inside your front door.

actions.title: Report broken alarms, dead exit lights and propped fire doors
actions.why: Shared fire protection only works if faults are reported, and the person who notices is usually a resident.
actions.how: Whenever you see a silent or chirping alarm, a dark exit sign or stair light, a stair door that is locked, wedged open or does not latch, or a blocked exit, report it to management in writing the same day, with the location, the date and a photo. Keep a copy. If it is not fixed, call your fire department's non-emergency or fire prevention number, or your city's housing inspection office.
actions.done: Each fault you have seen is reported to management in writing with its location, date and a photo, and you hold a copy.

actions.title: Know how a tall building moves in an earthquake
actions.why: High floors sway harder and longer than the ground shakes, and knowing that in advance stops the urge to run for the stairs.
actions.how: Expect the sway to be stronger the higher you live, and to go on after the ground has stopped. Drop, take cover under a sturdy table or against an inside wall away from windows and tall furniture, and hold on until the movement stops completely. Do not run for the stairs or the elevator while the building is moving. Afterwards put on shoes, check people, then check the building (HR-19), and use only the stairs.
actions.done: Everyone at home has heard this read aloud and has pointed to the sturdy table or inside wall where they would take cover.

region.label: Earthquake country
region.general: Outside earthquake country the same first move serves for any sudden jolt or blast in a tall building: get low, get away from glass, stay put until it stops, then check before you move.

actions.title: Check for damage after any shaking before you decide to stay
actions.why: A sound building is usually the best place to shelter and a damaged one is not, and the official inspection may be days away.
actions.how: Once the shaking stops, look over your unit, hallway and stairwell for damage: new cracks in walls, columns or beams, doors or windows that no longer close, sagging ceilings or floors, and water coming through. If you smell gas or hear hissing, stop checking and follow the gas steps (AR-13). If the building is damaged, or you are not sure, take your bag, leave by the stairs, move away from the building, tell management, and do not go back in until it has been inspected. If the damage is minor and nothing structural is affected, staying home is usually the better choice and leaves shelter space for people who have lost theirs. Do not flush until the drains are checked (X5-01).
actions.done: Every adult at home has read the list of damage signs or heard it read aloud.

region.label: Earthquake country
region.general: After an explosion, a vehicle impact, a fire, a flood or a severe storm, make the same checks before deciding to stay.

actions.title: Know the risks of living on a low floor
actions.why: The lowest floors are where sewage backs up, flood water arrives and stored belongings get soaked.
actions.how: If you live on one of the lowest floors: when the building is told not to flush, or after an earthquake or flood, plug the bath, shower and sink drains, because waste flushed upstairs can come out of the lowest fittings if a pipe is damaged. Keep documents, electronics and your emergency supplies at least 6 inches off the floor, and keep none of them in a basement storage locker. Ask management whether the first floor or basement has flooded before, and where the water came in.
actions.done: Documents, electronics and emergency supplies sit at least 6 inches off the floor, none is in a basement locker, and management has answered about past flooding.

actions.title: Find out how your car gets out of the garage with no power
actions.why: Electric gates and mechanical parking systems stop in an outage, and a car shut behind one is no part of your plan until you know the manual way out.
actions.how: Ask management: does the garage gate have battery backup, where is its manual release and who may use it, and do the garage lights and ventilation fans run on backup power. A car in a mechanical stacker or car elevator cannot be fetched without power. If a storm, heat wave or planned shut-off is forecast and you may need the car, park it outside the garage beforehand. Never sit in a garage with the engine running to charge a phone or keep warm. Write the answers on the Building information sheet by hand.
actions.done: Management's answers about the garage gate, its manual release, lights and fans are written on the Building information sheet.

actions.title: Carry heavy supplies up before you need them
actions.why: Once the elevators stop, every gallon of water and every can has to come up the stairs on somebody's back.
actions.how: Build your water and food stock a little at a time on normal shopping trips while the elevators work; do not plan to fetch it later. Water weighs about 8.3 lb a gallon, so 14 days for one person is about 116 lb. When a storm, heat wave or planned shut-off is forecast, top up that day. If you do have to carry during an outage, keep each load to about 20 lb and share the work with neighbors (see X4-04).
actions.done: The first load of extra water or food from a normal shopping trip is in your home.

actions.title: Charge e-bikes and scooters away from your exit
actions.why: A lithium battery fire near your door can cut off your only way out.
actions.how: Charge e-bikes, e-scooters and their batteries in a spot that is not between you and your front door, and never in the hallway or stairwell; outdoors and away from the building is safest where that is allowed. Use only the charger made for the device or one compatible with it, and unplug it once the battery is full. Store batteries out of direct sun and away from anything that can burn. Stop using a battery that swells, leaks, gets very hot, smells odd, changes color or makes odd noises. If the building has a charging or bike room, use it.
actions.done: Every e-bike, scooter and battery in your home charges in a spot that is not between you and your front door.

actions.title: Check which windows open, how far, and whether they are child-safe
actions.why: Windows are your ventilation and your signal to fire crews, and above the first floor they are a serious fall risk for small children.
actions.how: Twice a year, try every window and note which ones open, how far, and whether any are painted or screwed shut. The room you would shelter in needs at least one that opens, for cooling at night (HC-04) and for signaling in a fire (HR-07). If your windows do not open, or open only a few inches, you cannot cool the home at night. Write that on the Our reasons to leave sheet (X2-05) and plan to leave a summer outage on the first day the room passes your heat limit, about 88 °F (31 °C) if anyone at higher risk lives with you. If young children live with you or visit, check that windows above the first floor have guards, or stops that keep the opening to 4 inches or less, and keep beds, chairs and other climbable furniture away from them; an insect screen will not stop a fall. Report broken latches, guards or stops to management in writing.
actions.done: Every window has been tried and the result noted, a reminder is set for the next check, and any broken latch, guard or stop is reported in writing.

actions.title: Find out who can shut off the building's utilities
actions.why: The building's main gas, water and electrical lines are not yours to operate, so in a leak or flood what counts is how fast you can reach the person who can.
actions.how: Ask management who shuts off the building's gas, water, electricity and sprinkler system (the superintendent, a building engineer or the utility), who the backup is, and which number reaches them at any hour. Ask too how residents are told that a utility has been shut off and when it is back. Write the names and numbers on the Building information sheet by hand. Never try to work the meters, risers, pumps, sprinkler valves or main switchgear yourself; for a gas smell, leave and call from outside (see AR-13).
actions.done: The names and numbers of the people who shut off the building's gas, water, electricity and sprinklers, and their backup, are written on the Building information sheet.

actions.title: Check that your insurance pays for living somewhere else
actions.why: If your unit is unusable for weeks, somewhere else to live is the largest cost you will face, and the building's own policy does not cover it.
actions.how: Read your renters policy, or call the insurer, and find the coverage for living elsewhere, often called additional living expenses or loss of use. Write down its limit in money and in time, and what triggers it: damage to your unit only, or also an evacuation order or a long utility failure. Note what is excluded; flood and earthquake usually need separate coverage. The policy held by the building or the owners' association covers the structure, not your belongings or your costs of moving out. Record the details by hand on the Insurance and legal list (see MD-05).
actions.done: The limit in money and time, the triggers and the exclusions of your coverage for living elsewhere are written on the Insurance and legal list.

actions.title: Ask what the building stores for emergencies, and where
actions.why: Supplies the building already holds change what you need to keep yourself, but only if you know they exist and can get to them.
actions.how: Ask management or the residents' association whether the building keeps any of these: drinking water, portable toilets or toilet bags, lights, first-aid supplies, extinguishers, a cart, a stair chair, a generator. Ask which floors they are on, who holds the key, and when they were last checked. If there is nothing, raise it through the association (see NB-06); guidance written for tall buildings suggests stores on several floors, because supplies are hard to carry up. Note the answers on the Building information sheet by hand.
actions.done: The answers on what the building stores, on which floors and who holds the key are noted on the Building information sheet.

actions.title: Find out the trash plan for when the chutes close
actions.why: When collection stops or the compactor has no power the chutes are closed, and bags left in hallways block exits and bring pests.
actions.how: Ask management what happens to trash if collection stops or the chute and compactor are out of use: where bags should go, and where a temporary store would be. Until you are told, keep trash in your unit: wet and dry apart, crushed, double-bagged, in a lidded can (see X5-06). Never leave bags in the hallway or stairwell. Never put sealed toilet bags down the chute or in the building's trash cans; store them apart and wait for local instructions (X5-04).
actions.done: Management's answer on where trash goes when the chutes close is written on the Building information sheet.

actions.title: Find out whether your building has refuge areas
actions.why: Some tall buildings have protected places to wait for firefighters, and they only help if you know which floor and which door.
actions.how: Ask management, or look in the fire safety plan, whether the building has any area of refuge, area of rescue assistance or refuge floor, where it is, and how people waiting there call for help. If there is one, walk to the one nearest your unit and note its location on the Building information sheet by hand. If your building has none, the place to wait is your own unit with the door closed (HR-07), or a stair landing that is clear of smoke if you have already reached the stairs.
actions.done: The answer on refuge areas is noted on the Building information sheet, and if there is one you have walked to the nearest.
actions.cite_todo: No registry source describes areas of refuge or refuge floors; an NFPA or ADA source is needed before saying more than 'ask your building'.

actions.title: Walk the stairs once a year
actions.why: Stair times change as children grow and adults age, and doors and lights that worked last year may not work now.
actions.how: Once a year, on a date you will remember, have everyone in the household walk down one stairwell to the street and back up, carrying their bag and wearing a headlamp. Time it and compare with your time from X1-02. Use the other stairwell the following year. On the way, check doors, lights and landings and report any fault (HR-17). Check it off by hand on the Annual review sheet (see MD-19).
actions.done: Everyone at home has walked one stairwell down to the street and back up this year, and it is checked off on the Annual review sheet.
